items.title: Constitutional Roots under Company Rule (1773-1858)
items.body:
## In one line

The seeds of India's Constitution lie in the laws the British Parliament passed to run the East India Company between 1773 and 1858.

## Why it is asked

APPSC often asks 'which Act introduced which first' — the first Governor-General, first budget, first attempt at an all-India civil service.

## From trader to ruler

- The **East India Company** arrived in **1600** under a charter of **Queen Elizabeth I**; in **1765** it gained **Diwani rights** (revenue + civil justice) over **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**, turning from trader to territorial power.

## Landmark Acts of Company Rule

| Act | Key contribution |
|---|---|
| **Regulating Act 1773** | First regulation of the Company; created **Governor-General of Bengal** (Warren Hastings, 1st); Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) |
| **Pitt's India Act 1784** | **Board of Control** to supervise political affairs → **double government** |
| **Charter Act 1813** | Ended trade monopoly (except tea & China); asserted Crown sovereignty |
| **Charter Act 1833** | Made GG of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** (Lord William Bentinck, 1st); centralised legislation |
| **Charter Act 1853** | Separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council; **open competition** for recruitment to the ICS (Indian Civil Services); extended Company rule without specifying any fixed period |

- These Acts progressively built the **centralised, law-governed administration** that the Constitution later inherited.

## Terms explained

- **East India Company (EIC)** — the English trading company that gradually became India’s ruler.
- **Diwani** — the right to collect revenue and run civil justice, which the Company got over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765.
- **Governor-General** — the single topmost British administrator in India.
- **ICS (Indian Civil Service)** — the senior administrative service that ran the country.

## TL;DR

- EIC arrived 1600 (charter of Elizabeth I); acquired Diwani of Bengal/Bihar/Orissa in 1765.
- Regulating Act 1773 created the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings) and a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
- Pitt's India Act 1784 set up the Board of Control, creating double government.
- Charter Act 1833 created the Governor-General of India, with Lord William Bentinck as the first.
- Charter Act 1853 separated legislative and executive functions and opened the ICS to competition.
keyPoints: EIC arrived 1600 (charter of Elizabeth I); acquired Diwani of Bengal/Bihar/Orissa in 1765.
Regulating Act 1773 created the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings) and a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
Pitt's India Act 1784 set up the Board of Control, creating double government.
Charter Act 1833 created the Governor-General of India, with Lord William Bentinck as the first.
Charter Act 1853 separated legislative and executive functions and opened the ICS to competition.
items.mnemonic: Charter Act ladder '1813-33-53' = end monopoly → GG of India → open ICS.

items.title: Crown Rule & the Road to Self-Government (1858-1947)
items.body:
## In one line

After 1858 the British Crown ruled India directly, and a chain of reform Acts slowly gave Indians more say until independence in 1947.

## Why it is asked

The 1909, 1919 and 1935 Acts are a dense source of one-mark 'which Act gave what' questions.

## Crown takes over

- After the **1857 revolt**, the **Government of India Act 1858** abolished the Company: the **Governor-General became the Viceroy**, and a Cabinet-rank **Secretary of State for India** (with a 15-member Council) was created.

## Growth of representative institutions

| Act | Distinctive feature |
|---|---|
| **Indian Councils Act 1861** | First inclusion of Indians (non-officials) in legislative councils |
| **Indian Councils Act 1892** | Councils could **discuss the budget** & question the executive |
| **Indian Councils Act 1909** (Morley-Minto) | **Separate electorates** for Muslims (communal representation) |
| **GoI Act 1919** (Montagu-Chelmsford) | **Dyarchy** in provinces (transferred vs reserved subjects) |
| **GoI Act 1935** | **Provincial autonomy**; **Federal Court**; RBI & Public Service Commissions |
| **Indian Independence Act 1947** | Two independent dominions, **India and Pakistan**; Constituent Assemblies empowered to frame constitutions; British paramountcy over **princely states** lapsed, so each could **join either dominion or remain independent** |

- The **1935 Act** supplied much of the **structural framework** of the Constitution; the **1947 Act** made the Constituent Assembly a **sovereign** body.

## Terms explained

- **Viceroy** — the Crown’s personal representative who ruled India after 1858.
- **Secretary of State for India** — the British Cabinet minister answerable for India, based in London.
- **Dyarchy** — a split of provincial subjects into ‘transferred’ (run by Indian ministers) and ‘reserved’ (run by the Governor).
- **Separate electorates** — seats for which only voters of one community could vote.

## TL;DR

- GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule, created the Viceroy and the Secretary of State for India.
- Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
- Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
- GoI Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy, a Federal Court and provided for the RBI and PSCs.
- Indian Independence Act 1947 created two dominions and empowered their Constituent Assemblies.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule, created the Viceroy and the Secretary of State for India.
Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
GoI Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy, a Federal Court and provided for the RBI and PSCs.
Indian Independence Act 1947 created two dominions and empowered their Constituent Assemblies.
Indian Independence Act 1947 let princely states join India or Pakistan or remain independent.
items.mnemonic: 'Morley-Minto = Muslim electorates; Montagu-Chelmsford = dyarchy' — both start with M-M.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Historical Background (Crown Rule)

items.title: The Constituent Assembly — Demand, Formation & Composition
items.body:
## In one line

The Constituent Assembly was the body of members that actually wrote the Constitution between 1946 and 1949.

## Why it is asked

Numbers (389 reduced to 299 members), dates and 'who proposed what' are repeated every year.

## Demand for a Constituent Assembly

- **1928**: **Motilal Nehru Report** — first major Indian attempt at a constitution.
- **1934**: **M.N. Roy** first proposed a **Constituent Assembly**.
- **1935**: Congress officially demanded it; **1940**: conceded in the **August Offer**.
- Finally **constituted in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan** (the **Cripps Mission, 1942** had only promised one after WWII).

## Composition

- Planned strength **389 seats** (292 provinces + 93 princely states + 4 Chief Commissioners' provinces); reduced to **299** after **partition**.
- Members **indirectly elected** by provincial assemblies via **proportional representation + single transferable vote**; princely-state members were nominated by rulers.
- **Elections July 1946**; roughly one seat per 10 lakh people.

## Terms explained

- **Constituent Assembly** — the elected body of members that actually wrote the Constitution.
- **Proportional representation with single transferable vote** — a voting method that gives seats roughly in proportion to the support each group has.
- **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)** — the British plan under which the Assembly was finally set up.

## TL;DR

- Idea of a Constituent Assembly first given by M.N. Roy (1934); Nehru Report was 1928.
- Assembly was constituted in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
- Planned strength 389 seats, reduced to 299 after partition.
- Members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies through proportional representation and single transferable vote.
- August Offer (1940) accepted the demand for a Constituent Assembly in principle.
keyPoints: Idea of a Constituent Assembly first given by M.N. Roy (1934); Nehru Report was 1928.
Assembly was constituted in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Planned strength 389 seats, reduced to 299 after partition.
Members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies through proportional representation and single transferable vote.
August Offer (1940) accepted the demand for a Constituent Assembly in principle.
items.mnemonic: Seat drop '389 → 299' = partition took 90 seats to Pakistan.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Making of the Constitution (Demand & Composition)

items.title: Working of the Assembly & Adoption of the Constitution
items.body:
## In one line

This is how the Assembly worked through its committees and finally adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949.

## Why it is asked

The adoption date against the commencement date (26 January 1950) is a classic trap.

## Key milestones

- **9 December 1946**: first meeting held; **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha** the **temporary President** (Muslim League boycotted).
- **11 Dec 1946**: **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** elected **permanent President**; **H.C. Mukherjee** Vice-President; **B.N. Rau** Constitutional Advisor.
- **13 Dec 1946**: **Objectives Resolution** moved by **Nehru**; passed **22 Jan 1947** — became the basis of the **Preamble**.
- **29 Aug 1947**: **Drafting Committee** formed under **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** (7 members).

## Who sat on the Drafting Committee

| Member | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** | Chairman |
| **N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar** | Member |
| **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** | Member |
| **K.M. Munshi** | Member |
| **Syed Mohammad Saadullah** | Member |
| **N. Madhava Rau** | Replaced B.L. Mitter |
| **T.T. Krishnamachari** | Replaced D.P. Khaitan (died 1948) |

**Don't confuse:** **Jawaharlal Nehru** and **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** were **NOT** members of the Drafting Committee. Nehru chaired the Union Constitution and Union Powers Committees; Prasad was the Assembly's President and chaired the Rules Committee.

## Committees & final adoption

- **8 major + 15 minor committees**; **11 sessions**. Major chairmen: Drafting–**Ambedkar**, Union Constitution & Union Powers–**Nehru**, States–**Nehru**, Provincial/Advisory–**Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**, Rules–**Rajendra Prasad**.
- Took **2 years, 11 months, 18 days**; cost about **Rs 64 lakh**.
- **Adopted 26 Nov 1949**, came **into force 26 Jan 1950**, with **395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules**.
- The original was **handwritten** by **Prem Behari Narain Raizada**.

## Don't confuse

The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (finalised and signed) but **came into force on 26 January 1950** (Republic Day). Adoption and commencement are two different dates.

## Terms explained

- **Objectives Resolution** — Nehru’s statement of the aims of the Constitution. It is regarded as the **philosophical foundation** of the Constitution because its ideals were later incorporated into the **Preamble**.
- **Drafting Committee** — the seven-member committee under Ambedkar that prepared the draft text.
- **Adoption vs commencement** — ‘adopted’ means signed and finalised (26 November 1949); ‘came into force’ means legally effective (26 January 1950).

## TL;DR

- First meeting 9 Dec 1946; Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary President, Rajendra Prasad permanent President.
- Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, passed 22 Jan 1947; basis of the Preamble.
- Drafting Committee (7 members) under Ambedkar was set up on 29 August 1947.
- Making took 2 years 11 months 18 days across 11 sessions, at a cost of about Rs 64 lakh.
- Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950, with 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; handwritten by Prem Behari Narain Raizada.
keyPoints: First meeting 9 Dec 1946; Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary President, Rajendra Prasad permanent President.
Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, passed 22 Jan 1947; basis of the Preamble.

Making took 2 years 11 months 18 days across 11 sessions, at a cost of about Rs 64 lakh.
Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950, with 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; handwritten by Prem Behari Narain Raizada.
Drafting Committee: Ambedkar (Chairman), Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K.M. Munshi, Saadullah, Madhava Rau, T.T. Krishnamachari; Nehru was not a member.

items.title: Borrowed Features of the Constitution
items.body:
## In one line

India's makers borrowed the best ideas from other countries' constitutions, and examiners test which idea came from where.

## Why it is asked

'Source country of a feature' is one of the most repeated polity questions.

## A 'bag of borrowings' — with an Indian synthesis

After studying more than 60 constitutions, the makers adapted the best features to Indian conditions. The **structural part** rests largely on the **Government of India Act 1935**.

| Source | Borrowed feature(s) |
|---|---|
| **United Kingdom** | Parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet system, bicameralism |
| **United States** | Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment, preamble |
| **Ireland** | Directive Principles of State Policy, nomination to Rajya Sabha, method of Presidential election |
| **Canada** | Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union, appointment of Governors |
| **Australia** | Concurrent List, joint sitting of Parliament, freedom of trade & commerce |
| **Germany (Weimar)** | Suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency |
| **erstwhile USSR** | Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice in the Preamble |
| **South Africa** | Procedure for amendment; election of Rajya Sabha members |
| **Japan** | Procedure established by law |

- These borrowings were **modified**, not copied — Ambedkar defended this synthesis in the Assembly.

## Terms explained

- **Borrowed features** — ideas taken from other countries’ constitutions and adapted to Indian conditions, not copied.
- **DPSP (Directive Principles of State Policy)** — non-enforceable guidelines the State should follow, borrowed from Ireland.
- **Residuary powers** — the power to make laws on subjects not listed anywhere; in India these rest with the Union.
- **Judicial review** — the courts’ power to test whether a law agrees with the Constitution.

## TL;DR

- Parliamentary system, rule of law and single citizenship are borrowed from the United Kingdom.
- Fundamental Rights and judicial review are borrowed from the United States.
- Directive Principles of State Policy are borrowed from Ireland.
- Federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Union are borrowed from Canada.
- Emergency provisions (Germany-Weimar), Fundamental Duties (USSR) and the amendment procedure (South Africa) are other key borrowings.
keyPoints: Parliamentary system, rule of law and single citizenship are borrowed from the United Kingdom.
Fundamental Rights and judicial review are borrowed from the United States.
Directive Principles of State Policy are borrowed from Ireland.
Federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Union are borrowed from Canada.
Emergency provisions (Germany-Weimar), Fundamental Duties (USSR) and the amendment procedure (South Africa) are other key borrowings.
items.mnemonic: 'UK-US-Ireland' = Parliament - Rights - Directives (the three big pillars).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Historical Background / Making of the Constitution (Borrowed Provisions)

items.title: Exam-Precision Facts: Acts, Missions & the 1950 Status
items.body:
## In one line

A tight set of exact facts — colonial Acts, British missions and India's 1950 status — that past papers have asked almost word for word.

## Why it is asked

These are the precise details that decide one-mark questions.

## Dyarchy under the GoI Act 1919 - which subjects were Reserved?

Provincial subjects were split into two lists. **Reserved** subjects were administered by the Governor with his Executive Council (not answerable to the legislature); **Transferred** subjects went to Indian ministers responsible to the legislature.

| Category | Subjects |
|---|---|
| **Reserved** (Governor + Council) | **Administration of Justice, Land Revenue, Police**, irrigation, famine relief, press, prisons |
| **Transferred** (Indian ministers) | **Local Self-Government**, education, public health, agriculture, industries |

The 1919 Act also **clearly demarcated central vs provincial jurisdictions** and introduced **bicameralism** at the centre.

## GoI Act 1935 - the structural template

- **Residuary powers** were vested in the **Governor-General** (NOT the federal legislature).
- Provided **reserved seats for women**; established a **Federal Court (1937)**, **provincial autonomy** (abolished provincial dyarchy, introduced dyarchy at the centre), and separated **Burma**.

## The three missions

| Mission | Core proposal (exam trigger) |
|---|---|
| **Cripps Mission 1942** | Dominion status **after** WWII; a Constituent Assembly partly **elected by provincial assemblies + princely-state nominees**; any province **not accepting** the new Constitution could **retain its status / sign a separate agreement** with Britain (a 'post-dated cheque') |
| **Cabinet Mission 1946** | Recommended a **federal government** (Union of provinces + princely states) with **grouping of provinces**; framed the Constituent Assembly. It did **NOT** enlarge the powers of Indian courts or add more Indians to the ICS |
| **Simon Commission 1927-28** | **All-white**, with **no Indian member** -> nationwide boycott ('Simon Go Back') |

## Crown-era landmarks & the 1950 status

- **Charter Act 1813**: ended the Company's trade monopoly **except tea and trade with China**; asserted **Crown sovereignty**; earmarked Rs 1 lakh for education. It did **NOT** place Indian revenues under the British Parliament.
- **Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858**: disclaimed any intention to **annex Indian (princely) States**, placed administration **under the Crown**, promised religious toleration; it did **not** regulate Company trade.
- **Butler Committee 1927**: examined **relations between the Government of India and the princely States**.
- **Custodian of the Constitution** = the **Supreme Court of India**.
- **Status on 26 January 1950** = a **Sovereign Democratic Republic**. **Socialist** and **Secular** were added only by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.

## Terms explained

- **Reserved vs Transferred subjects** — under the 1919 Act, areas kept with the Governor versus those handed to Indian ministers.
- **Residuary powers** — power over subjects not named in any list; under the 1935 Act they lay with the Governor-General.
- **‘Post-dated cheque’** — the nickname for the Cripps Mission’s promise of self-rule only after the war.
- **Custodian of the Constitution** — the Supreme Court of India, which finally interprets it.

## TL;DR

- GoI Act 1919 Reserved subjects were Administration of Justice, Land Revenue and Police; Local Self-Government was a Transferred subject.
- Under the GoI Act 1935 residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General, not the federal legislature.
- Cripps Mission (1942) allowed any province not accepting the new Constitution to retain its status or sign a separate agreement with Britain.
- Cabinet Mission (1946) recommended a federal government with grouping of provinces; it did not enlarge court powers or add Indians to the ICS.
- Charter Act 1813 ended the Company monopoly except tea and China trade and asserted Crown sovereignty, but did not put Indian revenues under the British Parliament.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1919 Reserved subjects were Administration of Justice, Land Revenue and Police; Local Self-Government was a Transferred subject.
Under the GoI Act 1935 residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General, not the federal legislature.
Cripps Mission (1942) allowed any province not accepting the new Constitution to retain its status or sign a separate agreement with Britain.
Cabinet Mission (1946) recommended a federal government with grouping of provinces; it did not enlarge court powers or add Indians to the ICS.
Charter Act 1813 ended the Company monopoly except tea and China trade and asserted Crown sovereignty, but did not put Indian revenues under the British Parliament.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) disclaimed annexation of Indian States and placed administration under the Crown.
The Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted because it had no Indian member; the Butler Committee (1927) dealt with Crown-princely states relations.
On 26 January 1950 India's status was a Sovereign Democratic Republic; 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

items.title: Company-Rule Acts 1773–1853 — Every Provision
items.body:
## Company-rule Acts, provision by provision

**In one line:** between 1773 and 1853 the British Parliament passed six laws that turned a trading company into a regulated government, and each law left one or two "firsts" that examiners love.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC and UPSC frame statement questions from the smaller provisions too — who was subordinate to whom, which Act allowed missionaries, which Act was the last Charter Act.

**The story**

### Regulating Act, 1773
| Provision | Detail |
|---|---|
| First step | The **first step** of the British Government to **regulate** the East India Company; it **recognised** the Company's **political and administrative** functions and laid the foundation of **central administration** |
| Governor-General of Bengal | **Warren Hastings** was the first; assisted by an **Executive Council of four** members |
| Subordination | Governors of **Bombay and Madras** were made **subordinate** to the Governor-General of Bengal |
| Supreme Court | Set up at **Calcutta (Fort William) in 1774** with **one Chief Justice and three judges**; Sir **Elijah Impey** was the first Chief Justice |
| Conduct rules | Company servants were **prohibited** from **private trade** and from accepting **bribes** or presents |
| Reporting | The **Court of Directors** had to report its **revenue, civil and military** affairs to the British Government |

### Amending Act, 1781 (Act of Settlement)
- Exempted the **Governor-General and Council** from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for acts done in their **official capacity**.
- **Excluded revenue matters** from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.
- Required the court to respect the **personal law** of **Hindus and Muslims**.

### Pitt's India Act, 1784
- Distinguished the Company's **commercial** functions (left with the **Court of Directors**) from its **political** functions (given to a new **Board of Control**) — the system of **double government**.
- For the first time the Company's territories were called the **"British possessions in India"**.

### Charter Act, 1793
- Extended the Company's **trade monopoly** for another **20 years**.
- Gave the Governor-General **overriding powers** over the Bombay and Madras governments, and let him **override his own Council** in special cases.

### Charter Act, 1813
- **Ended** the Company's trade monopoly in India, **except** the trade in **tea** and the trade with **China**.
- **Asserted the sovereignty** of the British Crown over the Company's territories.
- Allowed **Christian missionaries** to come to India; set aside **Rs 1 lakh** a year for **education** (promoting Western education).
- Empowered the local governments to **impose taxes** on persons.

### Charter Act, 1833 — the final step of centralisation
- The Governor-General of Bengal became the **Governor-General of India**, with all civil and military powers; **Lord William Bentinck** was the first.
- The Governor-General of India was given **exclusive legislative power**; Bombay and Madras **lost their legislative powers**. Laws made earlier were called **Regulations**; laws made under this Act were called **Acts**.
- **Ended the Company's commercial activities** — it became a purely **administrative** body.
- Tried to introduce **open competition** for civil-service jobs, but this was **negated** after opposition from the **Court of Directors**.

### Charter Act, 1853 — the last Charter Act
- **Separated** the **legislative and executive** functions of the Governor-General's Council: six new legislative members formed the **Indian (Central) Legislative Council**, which worked like a **mini-Parliament**.
- Introduced **open competition** for the **ICS**, opened to Indians too; the **Macaulay Committee (1854)** was appointed on the Indian Civil Service.
- Extended the Company's rule **without fixing any period** — a sign that Parliament could end it any time.
- Introduced **local representation**: **four** of the six new legislative members came from the governments of **Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra**.

**Remember it:** 1773 regulate → 1784 double government → 1813 monopoly ends (except tea/China) → 1833 centralise (GG of India) → 1853 separate legislature + open ICS.

## Don't confuse
- **Governor-General of Bengal (1773, Warren Hastings)** vs **Governor-General of India (1833, William Bentinck)** vs **Viceroy (1858, Canning)**.
- **1833** only *proposed* open competition (negated); **1853** actually **introduced** it.

**TL;DR**
- 1773: first regulation; GG of Bengal (Hastings) + council of four; Bombay/Madras subordinate; Supreme Court Calcutta 1774 (Impey).
- 1781: GG and council and revenue matters kept out of the Supreme Court; personal laws respected.
- 1784: Board of Control + Court of Directors = double government; "British possessions in India".
- 1793: monopoly extended 20 years. 1813: monopoly ends except tea/China; missionaries; Rs 1 lakh education.
- 1833: GG of India (Bentinck), Acts not Regulations, Company purely administrative. 1853: last Charter Act; legislative council; open ICS.
keyPoints: Regulating Act 1773: GG of Bengal with an Executive Council of four; Bombay and Madras subordinate; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) with one Chief Justice (Elijah Impey) and three judges.
Amending Act 1781 (Act of Settlement) kept the GG-in-Council and revenue matters out of the Supreme Court and respected Hindu and Muslim personal law.
Pitt's India Act 1784 called the Company's territories the 'British possessions in India'.
Charter Act 1793 extended the monopoly by 20 years; Charter Act 1813 allowed Christian missionaries and set aside Rs 1 lakh for education.
Charter Act 1833 was the final step of centralisation: exclusive legislative power to the GG of India; earlier laws were Regulations, later ones Acts.
Charter Act 1853 was the last Charter Act: Indian Legislative Council (mini-Parliament), open ICS competition, Macaulay Committee 1854, four members from Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.

items.title: Crown-Rule Acts 1858–1947 — Every Provision
items.body:
## Crown-rule Acts, provision by provision

**In one line:** after the 1857 revolt the Crown ruled India directly, and each later Act widened Indian participation one step — councils (1861), budget debate (1892), elections and separate electorates (1909), dyarchy (1919), provincial autonomy (1935), freedom (1947).

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2014–2022 asked Queen Victoria's Proclamation, the 1919 Reserved subjects, the 1935 residuary powers and women's seats; state PSCs ask the "first Indian" names.

**The story**

### Government of India Act, 1858 ("Act for the Good Government of India")
- Abolished the Company; the **Governor-General** became the **Viceroy** — **Lord Canning** was the first Viceroy.
- Ended **double government** by abolishing the **Board of Control** and the **Court of Directors**.
- Created the **Secretary of State for India** (a member of the British Cabinet) with a **15-member Council of India**.
- **Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858)**, read at Allahabad, disclaimed any intention to **annex** the princely States and promised **religious toleration**.

### Indian Councils Act, 1861
- Began associating **Indians** with law-making: the Viceroy nominated non-official Indians — in **1862 Lord Canning** nominated the **Raja of Benaras**, the **Maharaja of Patiala** and **Sir Dinkar Rao**.
- Started **decentralisation** by **restoring legislative powers** to **Bombay and Madras**; new councils followed in **Bengal (1862)**, the North-Western Provinces (1866) and Punjab (1897).
- Gave statutory recognition to Canning's **portfolio system** (1859).
- Empowered the Viceroy to issue **ordinances** in an emergency, valid for **six months**.

### Indian Councils Act, 1892
- Increased the **non-official** members; councils could **discuss the budget** and **ask questions** of the executive.
- Provided a **limited and indirect** form of election: members were **recommended** by **district boards, universities, municipalities, chambers of commerce** and **trade associations**.

### Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms)
- Named after **Lord Morley** (Secretary of State) and **Lord Minto** (Viceroy).
- **Enlarged** the councils — the Central Legislative Council grew from **16 to 60** members; members could ask **supplementary questions** and move resolutions on the budget.
- **Satyendra Prasad Sinha** became the **first Indian** to join the **Viceroy's Executive Council** (as Law Member).
- Introduced **separate electorates** for **Muslims** (communal representation) — so **Lord Minto** is called the **"Father of Communal Electorate"**.

### Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)
- Followed **Montagu's August Declaration (20 August 1917)** promising responsible government; named after **Edwin Montagu** (Secretary of State) and **Lord Chelmsford** (Viceroy).
- Demarcated **central and provincial subjects**; provincial subjects split into **transferred** and **reserved** — **dyarchy**.
- Introduced **bicameralism at the Centre** (an Indian Legislative Assembly and a Council of State) and **direct elections**.
- Required **three of the six** members of the Viceroy's Executive Council (other than the Commander-in-Chief) to be **Indians**.
- Extended communal representation to **Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans**; franchise based on **property, tax or education**.
- Created a **High Commissioner for India** in London; provided for a **Public Service Commission** (the **Central PSC, 1926**); **separated provincial budgets** from the central budget; a **statutory commission** to review it after **10 years**.

### The road to 1935
- The **Simon Commission** (appointed **November 1927**, **seven** British members, report **1930**) had **no Indian member**, so it was boycotted.
- **Three Round Table Conferences** (1930–1932) followed; Ramsay MacDonald's **Communal Award (August 1932)** gave separate electorates to the depressed classes, modified by the **Poona Pact (1932)**.
- The **Butler Committee (1927)** examined relations between the Government of India and the princely States (the Paramount power).

### Government of India Act, 1935
- A long Act of **321 sections and 10 Schedules**.
- Proposed an **All-India Federation** of provinces and princely States — it **never came into being** because the States did not join.
- Divided powers into **three lists**: **Federal (59 items), Provincial (54 items), Concurrent (36 items)**; **residuary powers** went to the **Governor-General**.
- **Abolished dyarchy in the provinces** and gave **provincial autonomy**; provided **dyarchy at the Centre** (never implemented).
- **Bicameralism** in **six of the eleven provinces** (Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and the United Provinces).
- Extended communal representation to the **depressed classes (Scheduled Castes), women and labour**, and gave **women reserved seats** in the legislatures; extended the franchise to about **10%** of the population.
- **Abolished the Council of India**; set up the **Reserve Bank of India**; Federal, Provincial and Joint **Public Service Commissions**; a **Federal Court (1937)**; separated **Burma**.
- Because the Constitution kept its federal scheme, Governor, emergency powers and PSCs, the 1935 Act is the **structural framework of the present Constitution**.

### Indian Independence Act, 1947
- Based on the **Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)**, after **Attlee's** announcement of **20 February 1947**; received royal assent on **18 July 1947**.
- Ended British rule from **15 August 1947**; created the dominions of **India and Pakistan**; **abolished the office of Viceroy** — each dominion got a **Governor-General** appointed on the advice of its cabinet.
- Made each **Constituent Assembly sovereign** and also its **legislature**; **abolished the office of Secretary of State for India**; British **paramountcy lapsed**, so princely States could join either dominion or stay independent.
- **Lord Mountbatten** was the first Governor-General of free India; **C. Rajagopalachari** was the **last** (and only Indian) Governor-General.

## Don't confuse
- **1919 = bicameralism at the Centre; 1935 = bicameralism in six provinces.**
- **1919 = dyarchy in provinces; 1935 = dyarchy at the Centre** (and provincial autonomy).
- **First Viceroy = Canning (1858); first Indian in Viceroy's Executive Council = S.P. Sinha (1909).**

**TL;DR**
- 1858: Viceroy (Canning), Secretary of State + 15-member Council of India; Proclamation of 1 Nov 1858.
- 1861: three Indians nominated (Benaras, Patiala, Dinkar Rao); ordinances; portfolio system. 1892: budget debate, indirect election.
- 1909: Morley-Minto; S.P. Sinha; separate electorates; Minto "Father of Communal Electorate".
- 1919: dyarchy; bicameral Centre; direct elections; Central PSC 1926; High Commissioner.
- 1935: 321 sections, 10 Schedules; three lists 59/54/36; provincial autonomy; RBI; Federal Court 1937.
- 1947: Mountbatten Plan; two dominions; Secretary of State abolished; Rajagopalachari last Governor-General.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1858: Lord Canning first Viceroy; Board of Control and Court of Directors abolished; Secretary of State with a 15-member Council of India; Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1 November 1858.
Indian Councils Act 1861: Raja of Benaras, Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao nominated; ordinances valid six months; portfolio system recognised.
Indian Councils Act 1892: budget discussion, questions, and indirect election through district boards, universities, municipalities and chambers of commerce.
Morley-Minto 1909: Central Council 16 to 60; Satyendra Prasad Sinha first Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council; Minto the 'Father of Communal Electorate'.
GoI Act 1919: bicameralism at the Centre, direct elections, High Commissioner in London, Central PSC 1926, provincial budgets separated.
GoI Act 1935: 321 sections and 10 Schedules; Federal (59), Provincial (54), Concurrent (36) lists; bicameralism in six provinces; Council of India abolished.
Indian Independence Act 1947: royal assent 18 July 1947; Secretary of State abolished; Rajagopalachari the last Governor-General.

items.title: Constituent Assembly — Elections, Members, Sessions & Other Functions
items.body:
## The Constituent Assembly in detail

**In one line:** the Assembly was elected in mid-1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan, met from December 1946, became sovereign in 1947, and besides writing the Constitution it adopted the flag, anthem and the first President.

**Why it is asked:** election numbers (208, 73, 211, 299), the reason for choosing 26 January, the provisions that started on 26 November 1949, and the Andhra members are favourite one-mark items.

**The story**

### Demand and plan
- The **Nehru Report (1928)** was drafted by **Motilal Nehru** with eight other members; the **Karachi session (1931)** of the Congress passed a resolution on **Fundamental Rights** and economic policy.
- **1934 M.N. Roy** proposed a Constituent Assembly → **1935** the Congress demanded it → **1938 Nehru** said it must be elected on **adult franchise** without outside interference → **1940 August Offer** (Viceroy **Linlithgow**) accepted it in principle → **1942 Cripps Mission** offered one after the war (rejected by the **Muslim League**).
- The **Cabinet Mission (1946)** — **Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander** — laid down the scheme under which it was formed. An **Interim Government** was set up on **2 September 1946** with **Nehru** as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council.

### Composition and the 1946 election
| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Total seats | **389** — **296** for British India (**292** Governors' provinces + **4** Chief Commissioners' provinces) and **93** for princely States |
| Basis | Seats roughly **one per 10 lakh** people, divided among **Muslims, Sikhs and General** communities by population |
| Election (July–August 1946) | **Congress 208**, **Muslim League 73**, small groups and independents **15** |
| Nature | **Partly elected and partly nominated** — provincial members were elected by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies by proportional representation through the single transferable vote; princely-State members nominated by rulers |
| After partition | Strength fell to **299** (229 provinces + 70 States, Laxmikanth) |

### Sittings
- **9 December 1946** — first meeting, attended by **211 members**, in the **Constitution Hall** (now the Central Hall of Parliament); the Muslim League **boycotted** it. **Sachchidananda Sinha**, the **oldest member**, was temporary President, following the **French practice**.
- **11 December 1946** — **Rajendra Prasad** permanent President; **H.C. Mukherjee** and **V.T. Krishnamachari** were the **two Vice-Presidents**; **B.N. Rau** was the Constitutional Advisor (he prepared the first draft in **October 1947**).
- **28 April 1947** — representatives of **six princely States** took their seats; more joined after the **Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)**.
- After the **Indian Independence Act** the Assembly became **sovereign** and also the first **legislature (Dominion Parliament)**; as a legislature it was chaired by **G.V. Mavalankar**, who became the first Speaker.
- **Draft published February 1948**; about **7,635** amendments were proposed and **2,473** actually discussed.
- **Three readings:** first **4–9 November 1948**; second **15 November 1948 – 17 October 1949**; third **14–26 November 1949**.
- **26 November 1949** — the motion on the Draft Constitution was declared passed; **284 members** signed the Constitution on **24 January 1950**, the **final session**.
- From 26 January 1950 the Assembly continued as the **provisional Parliament** until the first general elections of **1951–52**.

### Other functions of the Assembly
| Date | Act of the Assembly |
|---|---|
| **22 July 1947** | Adopted the **national flag** (designed from **Pingali Venkayya**'s flag) |
| **May 1949** | **Ratified** India's membership of the **Commonwealth** |
| **24 January 1950** | Adopted the **national anthem** and the **national song**; elected **Rajendra Prasad** the **first President** |

### Some provisions began on 26 November 1949
- **Citizenship, elections, the provisional Parliament, temporary and transitional provisions and the short title** came into force on **26 November 1949** — **Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393**. The rest began on **26 January 1950**.
- **26 January** was chosen because on that day in **1930** the **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence) day was celebrated, following the **Lahore session (December 1929)**.

### The document and its makers
- **Elephant** was the Assembly's **symbol (seal)**.
- **Prem Behari Narain Raizada** handwrote the English original in flowing italic; **Vasant Krishan Vaidya** calligraphed the **Hindi** version; **Nandalal Bose** and artists of **Santiniketan** decorated the pages.
- About **15 women** were members (e.g. Sarojini Naidu, Durgabai Deshmukh, Hansa Mehta, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur).
- **Ambedkar** is called the **"Father of the Constitution"** (also "Modern Manu").
- The framers studied the constitutions of about 60 countries; the total cost was about **Rs 64 lakh**.
- The Supreme Court of India is the custodian of the Constitution (its final interpreter and guardian).

### Important members (source text)
| Member | Remembered for |
|---|---|
| **Vallabhbhai Patel** | Home and Information & Broadcasting in the Interim Government; **Bardoli** satyagraha; integration of princely States; later **Deputy Prime Minister** |
| **Abul Kalam Azad** | Scholar of Arabic; opposed Muslim separatism; later first **Education Minister** |
| **Rajendra Prasad** | **Champaran** Satyagraha; **three times** Congress President; later first **President** |
| **H.C. Mookherjee** | Vice-President of the Assembly; later **Governor of West Bengal** |
| **Durgabai Deshmukh** | Women's activist; founder of the **Andhra Mahila Sabha**; later founder Chairperson of the **Central Social Welfare Board** |
| **Baldev Singh** | Panthic **Akali** leader; later **Defence Minister** |
| **K.M. Munshi** | Later Union minister; a founder of the **Swatantra Party** |
| **B.R. Ambedkar** | Drafting Committee chairman; first **Law Minister**; inspired the **Republican Party of India** |
| **Shyama Prasad Mukherjee** | Minister for **Industry and Supply**; Hindu Mahasabha; founder President of the **Bharatiya Jana Sangh** |
| **Jawaharlal Nehru** | Head of the Interim Government; first **Prime Minister** |
| **Sarojini Naidu** | Poet; later **Governor of Uttar Pradesh** |
| **Somnath Lahiri** | **Communist Party of India** leader; later West Bengal MLA |

### Andhra angle
- From the Andhra region: **Durgabai Deshmukh** (Andhra Mahila Sabha), **Pattabhi Sitaramayya** (chaired the **House Committee**), **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** (Drafting Committee member, born in **Nellore** district), **N.G. Ranga** and **Tanguturi Prakasam**.

## Don't confuse
- **211** members attended the first meeting; **389** was the planned strength; **299** the strength after partition; **284** signed.
- **Mavalankar** chaired the Assembly **as legislature**; **Rajendra Prasad** chaired it **as constitution-maker**.

**TL;DR**
- 389 seats = 292 + 4 + 93; 1946 election: Congress 208, League 73, others 15; 211 at the first meeting.
- Two Vice-Presidents: H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari; Sinha temporary President as oldest member (French practice).
- Flag 22 July 1947; Commonwealth May 1949; anthem, song and President 24 January 1950; 284 signatures.
- Articles 5–9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391–393 began 26 Nov 1949; 26 Jan honours Purna Swaraj (1930).
- Elephant symbol; Raizada (English), Vaidya (Hindi), Nandalal Bose (art). Andhra: Durgabai, Pattabhi, Alladi, Ranga, Prakasam.
keyPoints: 1946 election: Congress 208, Muslim League 73, others 15; 211 members attended the first meeting on 9 December 1946.
Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary President as the oldest member (French practice); H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari were the two Vice-Presidents.
As the Dominion legislature the Assembly was chaired by G.V. Mavalankar; it ratified Commonwealth membership in May 1949.
Flag adopted 22 July 1947; national anthem and national song adopted and Rajendra Prasad elected President on 24 January 1950; 284 members signed.
Citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament and transitional provisions (Articles 5-9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391-393) came into force on 26 November 1949.
26 January was chosen to honour Purna Swaraj Day (1930); the elephant was the Assembly's symbol.
Andhra members: Durgabai Deshmukh (Andhra Mahila Sabha), Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N.G. Ranga, Tanguturi Prakasam.

items.title: Committees of the Assembly & the Full Borrowed-Features Table
items.body:
## Committees and borrowed features — the complete lists

**In one line:** the Assembly split its work among 8 major and 15 minor committees, and it drew ideas from the 1935 Act and about ten foreign constitutions; examiners match committee to chairman and feature to country.

**Why it is asked:** "Who chaired the States Committee?" and "Which feature came from Australia/Weimar/Japan?" are among the most repeated polity one-markers.

**The story**

### Major committees
| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| **Union Powers Committee** | **Jawaharlal Nehru** |
| **Union Constitution Committee** | **Jawaharlal Nehru** |
| **States Committee** (committee for negotiating with the States) | **Jawaharlal Nehru** |
| **Provincial Constitution Committee** | **Sardar Patel** |
| **Drafting Committee** | **B.R. Ambedkar** |
| **Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas** | **Sardar Patel** |
| **Rules of Procedure Committee** | **Rajendra Prasad** |
| **Steering Committee** | **Rajendra Prasad** |

### Sub-committees of the Advisory Committee
| Sub-committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Fundamental Rights | **J.B. Kripalani** |
| Minorities | **H.C. Mukherjee** |
| North-East Frontier Tribal Areas and Assam Excluded Areas | **Gopinath Bardoloi** |
| Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (other than Assam) | **A.V. Thakkar** |

### Minor committees (exam-relevant)
| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Finance and Staff Committee | Rajendra Prasad |
| Ad-hoc Committee on the National Flag | Rajendra Prasad |
| Credentials Committee | Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar |
| House Committee | **B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya** |
| Order of Business Committee | K.M. Munshi |
| Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly | G.V. Mavalankar |
| Ad-hoc Committee on the Supreme Court | S. Varadachari |
| Committee on Chief Commissioners' Provinces | B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya |
| Expert Committee on Financial Provisions | Nalini Ranjan Ghosh |
| Linguistic Provinces Commission | **S.K. Dhar** |
| Special Committee to examine the Draft Constitution | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| Press Gallery Committee | Usha Nath Sen |

### Drafting Committee changes
- Set up on **29 August 1947** with **seven** members: **B.R. Ambedkar** (Chairman), **N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar**, **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar**, **K.M. Munshi**, **Syed Mohammad Saadullah**, **N. Madhava Rau** and **T.T. Krishnamachari**. **N. Madhava Rau** replaced **B.L. Mitter**, who resigned on health grounds; **T.T. Krishnamachari** replaced **D.P. Khaitan**, who died in **1948**.

### Borrowed features — full table
| Source | Features borrowed |
|---|---|
| **Government of India Act 1935** | Federal scheme, **office of Governor**, judiciary, **Public Service Commissions**, **emergency provisions**, administrative details |
| **Britain (UK)** | Parliamentary government, **rule of law**, legislative procedure, single citizenship, cabinet system, **prerogative writs**, **parliamentary privileges**, bicameralism |
| **United States** | Fundamental Rights, independence of the judiciary, judicial review, **impeachment of the President**, **removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges**, post of **Vice-President** |
| **Ireland** | Directive Principles, nomination of members to the **Rajya Sabha**, **method of election of the President** |
| **Canada** | Federation with a strong Centre, **residuary powers** with the Centre, appointment of **state Governors by the Centre**, **advisory jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court |
| **Australia** | **Concurrent List**, freedom of **trade, commerce and intercourse**, **joint sitting** of the two Houses |
| **Weimar Germany** | **Suspension of Fundamental Rights** during an Emergency |
| **Soviet Union (USSR)** | **Fundamental Duties**; ideals of **justice (social, economic and political)** in the Preamble |
| **France** | **Republic**; ideals of **liberty, equality and fraternity** in the Preamble |
| **South Africa** | **Procedure for amendment** of the Constitution; **election of Rajya Sabha members** |
| **Japan** | **Procedure established by law** |

- The **structural part** comes largely from the **1935 Act**; the **philosophical part** (Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles) from the **American and Irish** constitutions; the **political part** (cabinet government, executive–legislature relations) from the **British** constitution.

**Remember it:** "**A**ustralia = **A**ll-together list (Concurrent) + joint sitting"; "**J**apan = **J**ust by law (procedure established by law)"; "**W**eimar = **W**ar-time suspension of rights".

## Don't confuse
- The **States Committee** was chaired by **Nehru**; the **Provincial Constitution Committee** by **Patel**. (The source PDF lists Patel for both — standard references give Nehru for the States Committee.)
- **Liberty-equality-fraternity = France**; **justice (social, economic, political) = USSR**.

**TL;DR**
- Nehru: Union Powers, Union Constitution, States. Patel: Provincial Constitution, Advisory. Prasad: Rules, Steering, Finance & Staff, Flag.
- Sub-committees: FR – Kripalani; Minorities – H.C. Mukherjee; North-East – Bardoloi; Excluded areas – Thakkar.
- House Committee – Pattabhi Sitaramayya; Credentials – Alladi; Order of Business – Munshi; Linguistic Provinces – S.K. Dhar.
- 1935 Act: Governor, PSCs, emergency. UK: writs, privileges. US: impeachment, Vice-President. Canada: advisory jurisdiction.
- Australia: Concurrent List, joint sitting. France: republic, liberty-equality-fraternity. Japan: procedure established by law.
keyPoints: Nehru chaired the Union Powers, Union Constitution and States Committees; Patel the Provincial Constitution and Advisory Committees; Prasad the Rules of Procedure and Steering Committees.
Advisory sub-committees: Fundamental Rights – J.B. Kripalani; Minorities – H.C. Mukherjee; North-East – Gopinath Bardoloi; Excluded Areas – A.V. Thakkar.
House Committee – Pattabhi Sitaramayya; Credentials – Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar; Order of Business – K.M. Munshi; Linguistic Provinces Commission – S.K. Dhar.
N. Madhava Rau replaced B.L. Mitter and T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan in the Drafting Committee.
From the 1935 Act: office of Governor, PSCs, emergency provisions; from the UK: prerogative writs and parliamentary privileges; from the US: impeachment of the President and the Vice-President.
Australia: Concurrent List, joint sitting, freedom of trade; Weimar: suspension of FRs; France: republic and liberty-equality-fraternity; Japan: procedure established by law.

items.title: For Mains — Evolution of the Indian Constitution
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance)

The evolution theme is rarely a bare 'list the Acts' question; examiners want you to **argue how far colonial statutes shaped — and how far the framers departed from — the 1950 Constitution**. Build every answer around continuity vs. break.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Colonial continuity** | Federal three-list scheme, office of Governor, emergency-type provisions, public-service structure, written exhaustive form — all traced to the **GoI Act 1935** (nearly 2/3 of provisions, incl. 250+ articles, drawn from it) |
| **Democratic break** | Popular sovereignty, universal adult franchise, justiciable Fundamental Rights, secular republic — things no colonial Act gave |
| **Synthesis** | 'Bag of borrowings' from 60+ constitutions, adapted not copied (Ambedkar's defence in the Assembly) |
| **Representativeness** | Indirectly elected, Congress-dominated, League boycott — yet inclusive of all communities, women, minorities (Granville Austin's microcosm) |
| **Criticism / limitations** | 'Lawyer's paradise', too bulky, borrowed, un-Gandhian (no village-republic base), elite-driven |
| **Way forward / relevance** | A 'living document' — basic-structure doctrine lets it evolve without losing identity |

**Data / authorities to quote:** Granville Austin, *The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation*; GoI Act 1935 as structural source; Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946) → Preamble; Ambedkar's 'Constitution is a vehicle of life' and 'if things go wrong it is because man is vile' speeches; 299 members, 11 sessions, 2y 11m 18d; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) for the living-document point.

**AP angle:** the Constituent Assembly's commitment to linguistic justice fed directly into the demand that produced the first linguistic state — **Andhra (1 Oct 1953)** after Potti Sriramulu's sacrifice — and the States Reorganisation Act 1956; a neat bridge from constitution-making to AP's own creation.

**Use in answers:** open by framing the Constitution as 'an evolutionary, not revolutionary, document'; use a two-column continuity/break mini-table; quote Austin's microcosm line; close with the living-document idea to show maturity. A simple timeline diagram (1773 → 1858 → 1919 → 1935 → 1950) earns easy structure marks.
keyPoints: Frame answers as continuity (GoI Act 1935 structural base) vs. break (sovereignty, FRs, adult franchise).
GoI Act 1935 supplied the bulk of structural provisions — federalism, Governor, emergency, three lists.
Quote Granville Austin (microcosm of a nation) and Ambedkar's Assembly speeches as authorities.
Representativeness critique: indirect election, Congress dominance, League boycott vs. inclusive spirit.
AP angle: constitutional commitment to linguistic justice led to Andhra (1953) and SRA 1956.
Close with the 'living document' idea anchored by Kesavananda Bharati's basic-structure doctrine.
